html:
The Paĩ Tavyterã of eastern Paraguay and the Kaiowá of Mato Grosso do Sul in Brazil are one Guarani people split by a border. Tekohá means the land where people can live their own way of life; the word sits at the centre of their claims to land.

They were forest farmers who grew maize and manioc in clearings and lived in large communal houses. Unlike many Guarani they were mostly outside the Jesuit missions. In the 1900s ranchers and soy farmers took most of their forest, and many Kaiowá were pushed onto small reserves. Their fight to return to their tekohá has led to violent clashes with landowners in Brazil. Their relatives include the Guarani and Ñandeva, and the Mbya further south.
